response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
The sale may be trademark infringement, but it depends on the circumstances. For example, use in trade by someone without permission can infringe if the mark is identical or deceptively similar, is used for goods covered by your registration, and is likely to be seen as a trademark. Offering goods for sale under the mark counts as use of the mark. [trade_marks_act_1999:29]

However, not every resale is infringement. For example, selling lawfully acquired goods that you or someone with your consent put on the market is not infringement merely for that reason. This protection does not apply if you have legitimate reasons to oppose further dealings, such as a change to or impairment of the goods after they were put on the market. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

The sources available do not explain what remedies you can seek or how to bring a claim. A trademark lawyer can help assess the facts and your options. This is legal information, not legal advice.

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, potentially. Even if your brand name is not registered, you may be able to bring a claim called “passing off” if someone uses an identical or deceptively similar trade mark. The law recognises passing-off protection for an unregistered mark used in business. [trade_marks_act_1999:11; trade_marks_act_1999:134]

A passing-off suit must be brought in a court no lower than a District Court with jurisdiction. Whether your particular claim would succeed depends on the facts; the sources provided do not set out all the requirements for passing off. [trade_marks_act_1999:134]

response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
Your application could be refused for several reasons. The answer depends on your mark and the goods or services in your application.

• It does not distinguish your goods or services from someone else’s, or it consists only of descriptive or customary terms. However, it may qualify if it became distinctive through use before you applied, or is well known. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It could deceive or confuse the public, hurt religious sensitivities, contain scandalous or obscene material, or be prohibited by the law on emblems and names. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It consists only of certain shapes, such as a shape necessary to achieve a technical result. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It conflicts with an earlier mark: the marks and goods or services are identical or similar in the combinations set out in the law, creating a likelihood of public confusion. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• It resembles an earlier mark well known in India, even for different goods or services, if using it without due cause would unfairly benefit from or harm the earlier mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• Its use could be prevented by copyright law or by the law protecting an unregistered mark used in trade, known as passing off. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

For the well-known-mark and passing-off or copyright grounds above, the source says an objection must be raised by the earlier mark’s owner in opposition proceedings. An earlier rights holder’s consent can also matter. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

The Registrar can refuse an application or accept it subject to changes or conditions. If it is refused or accepted conditionally, the Registrar must record the reasons and supporting materials in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
A trade mark registered under the Act is valid for 10 years and can be renewed for further 10-year periods. Each renewal runs from the expiry of the previous registration. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

To renew, the registered owner must apply to the Registrar in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed period, and pay the prescribed fee. The sources provided do not specify the form, fee or ordinary application deadline. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If you miss the expiry date, the Act provides for renewal within six months after expiry if the prescribed application, fee and surcharge are provided. If the mark has been removed for non-payment, restoration may be possible after six months and within one year of expiry, but it is subject to the Registrar being satisfied that restoration is just. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

International registrations at the International Bureau also last 10 years and can be renewed for 10-year periods. A six-month grace period applies, subject to a prescribed surcharge. [trade_marks_act_1999:36G]

response.question: Can I use a song in my YouTube video without permission?
response.answer:
Possibly, but you may need permission. It depends on the song and how you use it.

A use may be allowed without permission if it is a “fair dealing” for criticism or review, or for reporting current events or current affairs [copyright_act_1957:52]. Fair dealing means the circumstances of the use matter; calling a video a review does not automatically make the use fair.

Performers also have exclusive rights in certain uses of their performances [copyright_act_1957:38A]. The sources do not establish every situation in which permission is needed for a YouTube video, so I cannot say for certain without more details.

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
For a book published during the author’s lifetime, copyright generally lasts 60 years, counted from 1 January of the year after the author’s death. For example, if the author died in 2000, the 60 years run from 1 January 2001 through 31 December 2060. [copyright_act_1957:22]

If the book has joint authors, the period is counted from the year after the last author dies. [copyright_act_1957:22]

Different rules can apply. For example, if the book and any adaptation had not been published before the author’s death, the 60-year period can instead be counted from the year after first publication. An earlier publication of an adaptation can change the starting point. [copyright_act_1957:24] For a book published anonymously or under a pen name, the period generally runs from the year after publication, unless the author’s identity is disclosed before that period expires. [copyright_act_1957:23]

response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your job, the articles and any agreement you have with your employer. Writing an article at work does not, by itself, settle who owns it.

Generally, if you wrote the articles in the course of your employment under an employment or apprenticeship contract, your employer is the first copyright owner, unless you agreed otherwise. [copyright_act_1957:17]

A special rule applies if you worked for the owner of a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical and wrote the articles for publication in one. Unless you agreed otherwise, the owner is the first owner of the rights relating to publication in such periodicals and reproduction for that purpose. You are the first owner of the other copyright rights. [copyright_act_1957:17]

The available information is not enough to decide which rule applies to your articles.

response.question: Someone copied my book and is selling it. What legal action can I take?
response.answer:
If you own the copyright and the copies are infringing, selling them can amount to copyright infringement. Whether the copies infringe depends on the facts, including any permission or applicable exception. [copyright_act_1957:51; copyright_act_1957:52]

You can consider a civil case asking the court for an injunction—an order to stop the activity—and damages, meaning money for the harm suffered. You can also seek an account of profits. [copyright_act_1957:55]

The copyright owner can also take proceedings to recover possession of infringing copies. [copyright_act_1957:58]

There is a limit on monetary remedies if the defendant proves they did not know, and had no reasonable grounds to believe, that copyright existed in the work. In that situation, an injunction and a court-determined share of sales profits may still be available. [copyright_act_1957:55]

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?
response.answer:
For knowingly infringing copyright or helping someone else do so, the usual punishment is **six months to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business, the court may impose less than six months in jail or a fine below ₹50,000, but it must record special reasons. [copyright_act_1957:63]

For a second or later conviction for the same type of offence, the usual punishment is **one to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh. A similar exception applies where the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business. Certain older convictions do not count for this increased punishment. [copyright_act_1957:63A]

A separate rule applies to knowingly using a pirated computer program: the usual punishment is **seven days to three years in jail**, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If the program was not used for gain or in the course of trade or business, the court may, for special reasons, impose no jail sentence and a fine of up to ₹50,000. [copyright_act_1957:63B]

response.question: How do I register my copyright?
response.answer:
You can apply to the Registrar of Copyrights to enter details of your work in the Register of Copyrights. The author, publisher, copyright owner or another person interested in the copyright may apply. Use the prescribed form and pay the prescribed fee. [copyright_act_1957:45]

If your work is artistic and is used, or could be used, in relation to goods or services, the application must say so. It must also include a certificate from the Registrar of Trade Marks confirming that no identical or deceptively similar trade mark is registered in someone else’s name, and that no one else has applied to register one. [copyright_act_1957:45]

After receiving the application, the Registrar may make an inquiry and enter the work’s details in the register. [copyright_act_1957:45]

The sources do not give the form, fee amount, filing method or processing time.

response.answer: A patent generally lasts 20 years from the date the patent application was filed, not from the date it was granted. response.question: Who is allowed to apply for a patent?
response.answer:
A patent application may be made by:

- A person who claims to be the true and first inventor. [patents_act_1970:6]
- A person to whom that inventor has assigned the right to apply. [patents_act_1970:6]
- The legal representative of a deceased person who was entitled to apply immediately before their death. [patents_act_1970:6]

Any of these people may apply alone or jointly with another person. [patents_act_1970:6]

There is a restriction for nationals of countries specified by the Central Government in an official notification because they do not give Indian citizens equal patent rights. The supplied sources do not say which countries, if any, are currently specified. [patents_act_1970:134]

response.question: Can I file a patent in the US first if I live in India?
response.answer:
Yes, if you are resident in India, you can generally file a US patent application first only if you obtain a written permit from or on behalf of the Indian Patent Controller before filing. [patents_act_1970:39]

Alternatively, you can file for the same invention in India first, wait at least six weeks, and then file in the US, provided no relevant direction restricting the Indian application has been given, or all such directions have been revoked. [patents_act_1970:39]

For an invention relevant to defence or atomic energy, the Controller needs the Central Government’s prior consent to grant the permit. The restriction also does not apply to an invention first filed for protection outside India by a person resident outside India. [patents_act_1970:39]

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?
response.answer:
Yes. Someone may oppose your patent application or patent at different stages:

• Before grant: Once your application is published, but before the patent is granted, any person can submit a written opposition to the Controller, the patent authority. [patents_act_1970:25]
• After grant: An interested person can give the Controller notice of opposition after grant but before one year expires from the date the grant was published. An interested person includes someone engaged in or promoting research in the same field. [patents_act_1970:25; patents_act_1970:2]

Grounds for opposition include a claim that the invention was wrongfully obtained, that it was published before the relevant claim’s priority date, or that the patent description does not clearly and sufficiently explain the invention. The priority date is the date relevant to a particular patent claim. [patents_act_1970:25]

In a post-grant opposition, the Controller notifies the patent owner and refers the notice to an Opposition Board for examination and recommendations. After giving both sides an opportunity to be heard, the Controller can maintain, amend or revoke the patent. [patents_act_1970:25]

The sources describe these opposition routes; they do not establish whether other kinds of challenge may be available.

response.question: What exclusive rights does copyright give me over my novel?
response.answer:
If you own copyright in your novel, you generally have the exclusive right to do the following yourself or authorise someone else to do them, for the whole novel or a substantial part of it [copyright_act_1957:14]:

• Copy it, including storing it electronically [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Issue copies to the public, apart from copies already in circulation [copyright_act_1957:14]. A copy sold once counts as already in circulation [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Perform it in public or communicate it to the public [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Make a film or sound recording of it [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Translate it [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Adapt it, meaning make an altered version of it [copyright_act_1957:14].
• Exercise these rights in relation to a translation or adaptation [copyright_act_1957:14].

These rights are subject to the other provisions of the Act [copyright_act_1957:14].

response.question: Can I stop someone from distorting or mutilating my painting even after I sold it?
response.answer:
Yes, potentially. If you are the artist, you can seek to stop distortion or mutilation of your painting, or claim damages, if it would harm your honour or reputation. This right is independent of copyright and continues even if you have transferred the copyright. [copyright_act_1957:57]

The right does not mean you can prevent every change. Also, simply not displaying the painting, or not displaying it to your satisfaction, does not violate this right. [copyright_act_1957:57]

response.question: Is it a crime to sell fake branded goods?
response.answer:
Yes. Selling goods with a false trade mark or false trade description can be a crime. Offering them for sale or keeping them for sale can also be covered. [trade_marks_act_1999:104]

A false trade mark can include a brand mark, or a confusingly similar mark, applied to goods without the brand owner’s consent. [trade_marks_act_1999:102]

The seller is not automatically guilty just because the goods are fake. The law provides exceptions if the seller proves, for example, that they acted innocently, or that they took all reasonable precautions and had no reason to suspect the mark or description was not genuine. Another exception may apply if the seller gives the prosecutor all the information they have about their source when asked. [trade_marks_act_1999:104]

The punishment can be six months to three years in prison and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. A court may impose less than the minimum for special reasons recorded in its judgment. [trade_marks_act_1999:104]

response.question: What rights do I get once my patent is granted?
response.answer:
A granted patent gives you rights to stop certain activities in India without your consent:

• For a product patent, you can prevent others from making, using, offering for sale, selling or importing the product for those purposes. [patents_act_1970:48]
• For a process patent, you can prevent others from using the process. You can also prevent them from using, offering for sale, selling or importing for those purposes a product obtained directly by that process. [patents_act_1970:48]

These rights are subject to conditions and other provisions of the Act. For example, certain government use and use for experiments or research are permitted. [patents_act_1970:48] [patents_act_1970:47]

If you own the patent jointly, each owner normally has an equal undivided share, unless an agreement says otherwise. Subject to the relevant provisions and any agreement, one co-owner generally needs the others’ consent to grant a licence or transfer their share. [patents_act_1970:50]

This is legal information, not legal advice.

response.question: Can another company force me to let them make my patented medicine?
response.answer:
Yes, in some circumstances. Another company may be able to make your patented medicine under a compulsory licence granted by the Controller. This is permission to use the invention without the patent holder’s agreement. The company does not simply grant itself that permission. [patents_act_1970:90]

When setting the licence terms, the Controller must try to ensure that the payment to the patent holder is reasonable and that the licence is non-exclusive, meaning it does not give the licensee sole rights. [patents_act_1970:90]

response.question: A company copied my patented invention. What can a court order against them?
response.answer:
If you bring a patent infringement suit, the court may grant:

• An injunction: an order requiring the company to stop the infringing activity. [patents_act_1970:111]
• Damages: money for loss, or an account of profits: a financial remedy based on profits from the infringement. These are subject to restrictions. [patents_act_1970:109]

For example, damages or an account of profits cannot be granted if the company proves that, at the time of infringement, it did not know and had no reasonable grounds to believe the patent existed. [patents_act_1970:111]

The court may also refuse these financial remedies for infringement during a particular period following a missed renewal fee. [patents_act_1970:111] A further restriction can apply to use before an amendment to the patent specification was allowed. [patents_act_1970:111] These restrictions do not affect the court’s power to grant an injunction. [patents_act_1970:111]
